results.title: Tariffs may not bring global supply chains back; WashU research explains - The Source - WashU
results.content:
According to Kouvelis, these managerial decisions are not as straightforward as one might think. The product level and supply chain stage at which these tariffs are imposed makes a significant difference on their effectiveness in driving reshoring decisions, he said. [...] “However, persisting uncertainty together with limited reshoring capacity and cost discrepancies across production locations create ‘inertia’ in meeting market demand. As a result, global companies may continue to overflow excess demand to the offshore location.

“As a result, tariffs at any level — raw material, components and finished goods— end up increasing the cost of imported trade goods, at least in the short term,” he explained. [...] “This is especially true for industries like solar panels and electric vehicles (EVs) that are lacking strong domestic supply chains in upstream components, including ingots and wafers for solar panels, and batteries for EVs. Similarly, there is a slowdown in reshoring for U.S. bicycle manufacturers due to increased component-level tariffs.”

 Bonded warehouses: Store imported products while deferring duties until they leave the facility (quarterly harbor maintenance fees apply). [...] ## GaMEP Expertise
